title: Project scope management
exam_coverage_note: 8 of 60 marks. Joint second largest objective, alongside risk and issue management.
source_ref: APM PFQ Qualification Handbook, APM-QS-PFQ-8 V5 (April 2026), §11d. Syllabus maps this objective to APM Body of Knowledge 7th ed. 1.2.2, 1.2.3, 1.3.1, 4.1.4, 4.3.6, 4.3.7 and 8th ed. 2.5.1, 2.5.2, 2.6.1, 5.2.1, 5.7, 5.11.1, 5.11.3.
competence_area_note: The handbook publishes no per-objective Competence Framework mapping. Left null rather than guessed.
where_this_fits: Eight marks, and the point where the syllabus stops describing documents and starts describing control. Two of the eight outcomes are process lists that have to be recited, and they are the best value rote learning in the syllabus because the two lists are easy to mix up. Four more concern the breakdown structures.

key_definitions.definition: The process of identifying, defining and controlling the work required to deliver the project's objectives.
key_definitions.plain_english: Deciding what is in, what is out, and defending that boundary.

key_definitions.definition: A hierarchical decomposition of the products the project will deliver.
key_definitions.plain_english: The things being produced, broken into their parts.

key_definitions.definition: A hierarchical decomposition of the work required to produce the project's products.
key_definitions.plain_english: The jobs that have to be done, broken into manageable packages.

key_definitions.definition: A hierarchical decomposition of the project's costs.
key_definitions.plain_english: Where the money goes, broken down the same way the work is.

key_definitions.definition: A hierarchical decomposition of the people and organisational units involved in the project.
key_definitions.plain_english: Who is available to do the work, arranged as a structure.

key_definitions.definition: A matrix combining the work breakdown structure with the organisational breakdown structure to show who is responsible for each element of work.
key_definitions.plain_english: Work down one side, people across the top. Who does what.

key_definitions.definition: The process through which requested changes are identified, evaluated and then approved or rejected before implementation.
key_definitions.plain_english: The way a project decides yes or no to a change, rather than drifting into one.

key_definitions.definition: The process of identifying, recording and controlling the items that make up the project's outputs, and maintaining their status through the life cycle.
key_definitions.plain_english: Knowing which version of what is current, and keeping that record straight.

core_content.key_takeaway: Scope management is the process of identifying, defining and controlling the work required to deliver the project's objectives. Identifying establishes what has to be produced, defining pins it down precisely enough for someone to build it and someone else to accept it, and controlling keeps the boundary intact once work starts. Scope covers what is excluded as well as what is included.
core_content.body_markdown:
Three verbs, and each one matters.

Identifying establishes what needs to be produced. Defining pins it down precisely enough that someone can build it and someone else can accept it. Controlling keeps the boundary intact once work starts.

That third verb is where most of this objective sits. A project without scope control does not usually fail through one big decision. It fails through an accumulation of small additions that nobody priced, agreed or scheduled.

Recording what is excluded is not pedantry. Unstated exclusions are the most common source of the argument at handover.

core_content.outcome_title: Differentiate between scope management within linear projects and within iterative projects
core_content.key_takeaway: In a linear project the scope is defined in full and baselined before delivery begins, and any change to it goes through formal change control, with time and cost flexing to accommodate approved changes. In an iterative project time and resources are fixed for each iteration and the scope inside it is agreed and re-prioritised as the work proceeds. The real question is which constraint the project is prepared to move.
core_content.body_markdown:
Neither approach abandons control. What differs is the level at which change gets handled.

In a linear project, scope is the thing being protected. It is defined in full, baselined, and moved only by a formal decision. Time and cost are what give.

In an iterative project, time and cost are the things being protected. Requirements are expected to evolve, and the mechanism for handling that is re-prioritising what goes into the next iteration rather than raising a change request.

An iterative project still has a total budget, a deadline and a set of objectives. It is not an uncontrolled one.

core_content.outcome_title: Describe how product breakdown structures and work breakdown structures are used to illustrate the required scope of work
core_content.key_takeaway: A product breakdown structure decomposes the outputs and answers what is being produced. A work breakdown structure decomposes the work needed to produce them, ending in work packages small enough to be estimated, assigned and tracked. Products come first, then the work. Both structures are used in linear and in iterative projects.
core_content.body_markdown:
Both are hierarchical breakdowns used to make scope visible and manageable. What differs is what sits in the boxes.

A product breakdown structure starts with the final product at the top, breaks it into components, and those into sub components.

A work breakdown structure starts with the project and breaks it down into the work that has to be done, ending in work packages.

The usual order is products first, then work, because deciding what to build before deciding how to build it avoids the classic failure of a plan full of activity that produces nothing anyone asked for.

Both serve the same purpose: breaking something too big to grasp into pieces that can be estimated, allocated and reported on.

core_content.outcome_title: Outline how a project manager would use cost, organisational breakdown structures and the responsibility assignment matrix
core_content.key_takeaway: The cost breakdown structure decomposes the project's costs, normally mirroring the work breakdown structure so that cost can be reported at any level of the work. The organisational breakdown structure decomposes the people and organisational units available to the project. The responsibility assignment matrix combines the two, with work from the WBS down one axis and people from the OBS across the other, and each intersection recording who is responsible. Drawing the matrix exposes gaps and overlaps. Work with nobody against it, and work with three people against it, are both problems, and both stay invisible until the matrix is drawn.
core_content.body_markdown:
The equation is worth memorising. WBS multiplied by OBS produces the RAM. Questions usually test whether you know which two structures combine, and swapping in the CBS or PBS is the standard wrong answer.

The cost breakdown structure supports budgeting, cost control and reporting against the baseline.

The organisational breakdown structure shows which teams, departments or suppliers exist and how they relate.

The practical value of a responsibility assignment matrix is that it exposes both gaps and overlaps. Work with nobody against it, and work with three people against it, are both problems, and both stay invisible until the matrix is drawn.

core_content.outcome_title: Define 'configuration management' and 'change control' in the context of scope management
core_content.key_takeaway: Change control is the process through which requested changes are identified, evaluated, and then approved or rejected before implementation. Configuration management is the process of identifying, recording and controlling the items that make up the project's outputs, and maintaining their status through the life cycle. Change control evaluates and decides; configuration management identifies and records.
core_content.body_markdown:
Change control is a decision process. Its output is a yes or a no, with reasons.

Configuration management is a record keeping process. Its output is the certainty that everyone knows which version of what is current.

The pairing exists because each is useless on its own. Approving changes without recording them produces a project where nobody can say what the current design is. Recording versions without controlling changes produces an accurate history of an uncontrolled project.

The definitions are often offered as each other's answers, so learn them by their verbs. Change control evaluates and decides. Configuration management identifies and records.

core_content.outcome_title: Explain the relationship between change control and configuration management
core_content.key_takeaway: Change control decides whether a change should happen. Configuration management makes sure that once it has happened, the records reflect it and everyone is working from the current version. Approving changes without recording them leaves nobody able to say what the current design is, and recording versions without controlling changes produces an accurate history of an uncontrolled project.
core_content.body_markdown:
Run through a single change and the relationship is clear.

A request is raised. Change control evaluates its impact on scope, time, cost, quality and risk, and a decision is taken. If it is approved, the work is done. Configuration management then updates the affected items, increments their version, and records the new status. Anyone asking what the current specification is now gets the right answer.

Remove either half and the failure is specific. Without change control, changes get made with nobody assessing their impact. Without configuration management, approved changes get made but the documentation still describes the old version, and someone eventually builds or tests against the wrong one.

Updating the records is not administrative tidying. It is what makes the approval real.

core_content.outcome_title: Outline the stages in a typical change control process
core_content.key_takeaway: A typical change control process runs: a request for change is raised and logged, an initial evaluation decides whether it is worth assessing in detail, a detailed evaluation assesses the impact on scope, schedule, cost, quality, risk and benefits, a recommendation is made, a decision is taken by whoever holds the authority, and approved changes are implemented with the affected records and baselines updated. The project manager decides within their tolerance and the governance board decides beyond it. The process exists to prevent scope creep: change by accumulation, unpriced and unagreed.
core_content.body_markdown:
Take the stages one at a time.

The request is raised and logged, so that it exists as a record rather than a conversation.

The initial evaluation establishes whether the request is valid and worth assessing in detail. Some requests fail here, which saves the cost of a full assessment.

The detailed evaluation is the substance of the process. It assesses the impact on scope, schedule, cost, quality, risk and benefits, and it is where the true cost of a change usually turns out to be larger than the obvious one.

A recommendation is made on the basis of that evaluation, and a decision is taken by whoever holds the authority.

Implementation follows for approved changes, and the affected records and baselines are updated.

The reason the process exists is that the alternative is scope creep: change by accumulation, unpriced and unagreed.

core_content.outcome_title: Outline the activities in a typical configuration management process
core_content.key_takeaway: The five activities in a typical configuration management process are planning, identification, control, status accounting, and verification audit. Planning sets what will be controlled and by whom, identification gives each configuration item a unique reference, control ensures changes happen only through the agreed process, status accounting records the current state and change history of each item, and verification audit checks that the records match reality.
core_content.body_markdown:
Take the five in turn.

Planning establishes what will be placed under configuration management, how, and by whom. Not everything needs controlling, and deciding that boundary is the first activity.

Identification determines the individual configuration items and gives each a unique reference, so that a specific version of a specific thing can be pointed at without ambiguity.

Control ensures that changes to those items happen only through the agreed process.

Status accounting records and reports the current state of every item and its change history. It answers what version is current, and what happened to get here.

Verification audit checks that the records match reality. It is what catches the case where the documentation says version four and the thing built is version three.

Together the five produce one property: at any moment, the project can say what the current approved version of anything is, and prove it.

misconceptions.wrong: Scope management is just writing down what the project will deliver.
misconceptions.right: It is identifying, defining and controlling. Control is where most of the examinable content sits, and where projects actually fail.

misconceptions.wrong: Iterative projects do not control scope.
misconceptions.right: They control it by fixing time and cost and re-prioritising scope within them. Different mechanism, not an absence of control.

misconceptions.wrong: A product breakdown structure and a work breakdown structure are the same thing drawn differently.
misconceptions.right: One decomposes what is being produced, the other decomposes the work needed to produce it. Products first, then work.

misconceptions.wrong: The responsibility assignment matrix comes from the product breakdown structure.
misconceptions.right: It comes from the work breakdown structure combined with the organisational breakdown structure. Work by people.

misconceptions.wrong: Change control and configuration management are two names for the same process.
misconceptions.right: Change control decides whether a change happens. Configuration management records what the current version is. Each is useless without the other.

misconceptions.wrong: Configuration management is only about documents.
misconceptions.right: It applies to any configuration item the project chooses to control, including designs, software, physical components and documentation.

misconceptions.wrong: A change should be implemented as soon as it is approved, and the paperwork can catch up.
misconceptions.right: Updating the records is part of the process. Without it, the approved change exists in the product but not in the documentation, which is how the wrong version gets built or tested.

memory_aids.expansion: Planning, Identification, Control, Status accounting, Verification audit. The five configuration management activities, in order.
Change control decides. Configuration management records. Two verbs that resolve the most confused pair in this objective.
Work multiplied by people gives the responsibility assignment matrix. If an option names any other pair of structures, it is wrong.
PBS decomposes products. WBS decomposes work. Decide what before deciding how.

progress_checkpoint: I can define scope management using all three verbs, including control.
I can say how scope is handled differently in linear and iterative projects, and why.
I can explain the difference between a PBS and a WBS, and say which two structures combine to form a RAM.
I can define change control and configuration management without confusing them.
I can list the stages of a typical change control process in order.
I can name the five configuration management activities and tell, for any given word, which of the two lists it belongs to.

source_confidence.claim: The five configuration management activities are planning, identification, control, status accounting and verification audit.
source_confidence.basis: Named in the bracketed 'including' list in syllabus outcome 5.8. The handbook states bracketed content is examinable.

source_confidence.claim: A typical change control process runs request, evaluate, recommend, decide, implement, update.
source_confidence.basis: Derived from the APM Body of Knowledge sections referenced by this outcome, and consistent with the published sample paper, which tests individual stage names rather than the full sequence.
source_confidence.risk: The syllabus says 'a typical change control process', so wording varies between sources. Teach the shape and the stage names; do not present one provider's exact sequence as the only correct one.
